title: Study of the Integrated Biomechanics of the Lower Limbs and Trunk in Athletes of Different Age Groups During the Performance of Motor Tasks
official: Study of the Integrated Biomechanics of the Lower Limbs and Trunk in Athletes of Different Age Groups During the Performance of Motor Tasks
summary:
Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries, particularly non-contact injuries, are among the most common injuries in team sports and frequently occur during cutting maneuvers. They are associated with a substantial risk of secondary injuries, especially in pediatric and adolescent athletes. Persistent biomechanical alterations, neurocognitive deficits, and suboptimal movement strategies may contribute to the risk of re-injury even after ACL reconstruction and return to sport.

The diagnosis of ACL injury and the indication for surgical treatment are primarily based on clinical assessment, including tests such as the anterior drawer, Lachman, and pivot shift tests, which evaluate anteroposterior laxity and rotational instability. Instrumented assessments, including the KT-1000 and KiRA accelerometer, can provide objective measurements of knee laxity and complement the clinical evaluation.

Several ACL reconstruction techniques and graft types are currently available, with the main goal of restoring anteroposterior and rotational knee stability, recovering function, and reducing the risk of subsequent injury. Despite favorable clinical outcomes and high rates of return to sport, athletes may continue to show deficits in neuromuscular control, functional performance, and high-intensity movement patterns after rehabilitation and return to sport.

Conventional return-to-sport assessments may therefore fail to detect residual deficits, particularly during dynamic and sport-specific movements. This highlights the need for objective and multidimensional assessment methods capable of quantitatively evaluating movement quality under ecologically valid conditions.

Although optoelectronic motion capture systems represent the gold standard for movement analysis, their use is mainly restricted to controlled laboratory settings, which may not fully reproduce the demands and natural movement patterns of sports activities. In contrast, wearable inertial sensors and markerless motion analysis based on pose-estimation algorithms allow objective, non-invasive, and ecologically valid assessment of complex movements in both clinical and sporting environments.

Given the high risk of re-injury and the evidence of persistent biomechanical alterations following ACL reconstruction, investigating movement patterns during sport-specific tasks is therefore of particular interest. Integrating wearable sensors and markerless motion analysis and comparing ACL-reconstructed athletes with healthy individuals may help identify residual biomechanical and neuromuscular alterations that are not detectable through conventional clinical assessment alone.
